resources.note: Ask them for a reputable lawyer list.

getLawyer.why: You can be held up to 48 hours before seeing a judge, and cases can take years with detention throughout. Clearly ask police to contact the Embassy of Canada, demand a lawyer (a public defender if you can't afford one), and sign nothing without counsel. Beware 'pirate lawyers' near tourist police stations — get the embassy's lawyer list.

ZERO-tolerance — even a small amount brings severe penalties and long jail. Traffickers use tourists as unknowing couriers: never carry anything that isn't yours, never leave bags unattended, and expect searches (even X-ray) on departure. Contact the embassy and a lawyer immediately.

deadlines.title: Tourist stay — 30 days (extendable to 120)
deadlines.rule: No visa for tourist stays up to 30 DAYS; extendable by up to 120 days (apply at the Directorate General for Migration before your tourist card expires). Complete the e-ticket before boarding. Overstaying can mean deportation or refused re-entry.
deadlines.source: Government of Canada travel advice — Dominican Republic

deadlines.title: Victims must report BEFORE leaving the country
deadlines.rule: If you're a crime victim, you must file a formal complaint with local authorities BEFORE leaving the country, or the investigation won't proceed.
deadlines.source: Government of Canada travel advice — Dominican Republic

sentencing.name: Drug possession / trafficking (Dominican Republic)
sentencing.mandatory_minimum: Pre-trial detention is the norm and can last years.
sentencing.first_offender: Zero-tolerance: even a small amount can bring long jail terms and heavy fines; a local lawyer is essential.
sentencing.collateral: Lengthy pre-trial detention, deportation, re-entry bar.

statutes.title: Carry ID; roadblocks common
statutes.summary: Authorities can ask for ID any time; roadblocks are common (especially near the Haitian border). Carry your passport or a copy plus a separate copy of your entry stamp/visa.

statutes.title: Consular access + right to counsel
statutes.summary: If arrested, clearly ask to contact the Embassy of Canada; you have the right to a lawyer (a public defender if you can't afford one) who can be present during questioning and at trial.

book.title: Police, detention, and your rights in the Dominican Republic
book.overview: The DR is a civil-law country. You can be held up to 48 hours before seeing a judge, and the system is slow. Carry ID (roadblocks are common). If detained, insist on contacting the Embassy of Canada and a lawyer, and avoid the 'pirate lawyers' who target detained foreigners. Emergency: 911; Tourist Police (CESTUR) 1-809-200-3500.
your_rights: Authorities can ask for ID any time — carry your passport/copy.
If arrested you can be held up to 48 hours before a judge; you have the right to a lawyer (public defender if needed).
You can ask police/prison to contact the Embassy of Canada.
A lawyer may be present during questioning and at trial.
Do not sign anything without a lawyer and translation.
key_steps: Carry ID and a copy of your entry stamp.
If detained: clearly ask for the embassy and a lawyer; stay calm.
Use the embassy's lawyer list — avoid touts near tourist police stations.
If you're a crime victim, file a formal complaint BEFORE you leave the country.
common_mistakes: Hiring a 'pirate lawyer' who overcharges detained tourists.
Not reporting a crime before leaving (investigation won't proceed).
Signing Spanish documents you don't understand.
book.when_lawyer: If detained, arrested, or in any drug matter: contact the embassy and get a reputable local lawyer from their list immediately.

book.title: Entry, tourist card, and your stay in the DR
book.overview: No visa for up to 30 days (extendable to 120). Complete the e-ticket before boarding; the tourist card cost is usually in your airfare. Overstaying causes deportation or refused re-entry.
your_rights: Visa-free tourism up to 30 days; extend up to 120 days via Migration.
You need a new e-ticket for every trip.
You're entitled to your entry record.
key_steps: Track your 30 days; extend before the card expires.
Carry proof of funds, address, and onward travel if asked.
Keep copies of your passport and entry stamp.
book.when_lawyer: For overstays or residency, consult a DR immigration lawyer via the embassy.

sources.title: Government of Canada — Dominican Republic travel advice

book.title: Staying safe + the drug-courier trap
book.overview: Dial 911 for emergencies. The biggest legal traps for tourists: the drug zero-tolerance policy and being used as an unknowing courier. Never carry anything that isn't yours, never leave bags unattended, and expect departure searches. Report any crime before you leave.
your_rights: Call 911; Tourist Police (CESTUR) assist in tourist areas.
You can report crimes — but must do so before leaving to keep the case alive.
key_steps: Never carry others' bags/items; watch your luggage.
After a crime, file a formal complaint locally before departure.
Use hotel safes and registered transport.
In danger, call 911, then the embassy.
common_mistakes: Carrying a stranger's bag or gift.
Leaving the country without reporting a crime.
book.when_lawyer: For any detention, drug allegation, or serious crime, contact the embassy for a reputable lawyer.
